title: Chapter 37
paragraphs: Ferndean Manor was a building of considerable age, moderate size, and no architectural ambition, buried deep in a wood. I had heard of it before. Mr. Rochester often spoke of it and sometimes visited. His father had bought the estate for its hunting grounds. He would have rented the house but could find no tenant, because of its remote and unhealthy location. So Ferndean remained empty and unfurnished, except for two or three rooms fitted up for Mr. Rochester's occasional overnight stays.

I reached this house just before dark on an evening marked by grey skies, a cold wind, and steady, penetrating rain. The last mile I walked, having dismissed the carriage and driver with the double payment I'd promised. Even when I was very close to the manor, I could see nothing of it—so thick and dark were the trees of the gloomy wood around it. Iron gates between granite pillars showed me where to enter. Passing through them, I found myself among trees. There was no clear drive visible, no smooth lawn or broad walk. The growth of the surrounding woods had crept right up to the very doorstep. They were wild and untrimmed.

I thought I had taken a wrong turn and lost my way. The darkness of nature and forest gathered around me. I looked for another path. There was none—only interwoven branches, thick trunks, and dense summer foliage. Not an opening anywhere.

I kept going. At last the trees thinned a little. Soon I made out a railing, then the house—barely distinguishable from the trees in the dim light, so damp and green were its decaying walls. I entered through a door fastened only with a latch and stood in an enclosed yard from which the wood curved away in a half circle. There were no flowers, no garden beds—only a broad gravel walk circling a patch of grass, set in the heavy frame of the forest. The house presented two pointed gables in its front. The windows were latticed and narrow. The front door was narrow too—one step led up to it. The whole looked, as the innkeeper had said, "quite a desolate spot."
"Can there be life here?" I asked.
Yes—life of some kind was there. I heard a movement. That narrow front door was opening, and some shape was about to emerge.

It opened slowly. A figure came out into the twilight and stood on the step—a man without a hat. He stretched out his hand as if to feel whether it was raining. Dark as it was, I recognized his strong shape and features. I nearly revealed myself—but I held back. I was not yet ready to meet him. I had still a thing or two to think through. I needed to prepare myself for the shock—and to prepare him.

I stayed where I was, barely breathing, and watched him—studied him, unseen, and sadly invisible to him. It was a meeting in the dark. I held back the tears that threatened and willed my heart to steady itself.

His form was the same strong, powerful build as ever. His bearing was still upright. His hair was still raven-black. His features were still sharp and firm. Not in one year's time had decay advanced so far as to alter either. But in his face I saw a change—a look of desperate brooding that reminded me of some wronged and chained wild animal. The sightless eyes were tragic to behold. They were dark, and wild, and hopeless.

And, reader, do you think I feared him in his blind fury? If you do, you don't know me. A gentle hope blended with my sorrow. I could feel his heart was still warm, still beating, still mighty. I was sure I could bring him comfort. I just needed to find the right approach.

He stepped down from the doorstep and moved slowly, gropingly, toward the grass. Where was his bold stride now? He felt his way cautiously, as one who walks in darkness. He stopped. He stood still. Then he stretched out his right hand—the hand that had no fingers—toward the sky, the trees, the rain. He seemed to gather the elements in that mutilated grasp. He tried to see with those blind eyes. He let his hand fall, then turned and went back inside.
"Will you take my arm, sir?" said a voice. It was John. "There's a heavy shower coming on. You'd better go in."
"Leave me alone," was the answer.
John withdrew without noticing me. Mr. Rochester tried again to walk about—in vain. Everything was too uncertain. He groped his way back to the house and re-entered it. I heard him close the door.
I now approached and knocked. John's wife opened for me. "Mary," I said, "how are you?"

She started as if she had seen a ghost. I calmed her. To her flustered "Is it really you, miss, come at this late hour to this lonely place?" I answered by taking her hand. Then I followed her into the kitchen, where John now sat by a good fire. I explained in a few words that I had heard everything that had happened since I left Thornfield, and that I had come to see Mr. Rochester. I asked John to go down to the inn at Millcote and fetch my trunk, which I had left there. I then sat down to collect my thoughts and consider how best to approach my master.
"When you go in," I said, "tell your master that a person wishes to speak to him, but don't give my name."
"I don't think he'll see you," she answered. "He refuses everybody."
When she returned, I asked what he had said.
"You are to send in your name and your business," she replied. She then proceeded to fill a glass with water and place it, with candles, on a tray. I noticed her hand was shaking.
"Is that what he rang for?" I asked.
"Yes. He always has candles brought in at dark, even though he's blind."
"Give the tray to me. I will carry it in."
I took it from her hand. She pointed me toward the parlour door. The tray shook as I held it. The water sloshed from the glass. My heart pounded. Mary opened the door for me and shut it behind me.

The parlour looked grim. A neglected handful of fire burned low in the grate. Leaning over it, with his head propped on his hand, sat the blind tenant of the room. His old dog, Pilot, lay on one side, curled up as if afraid of being accidentally stepped on. Pilot pricked his ears when I came in. Then he jumped up with a yelp and bounded toward me. He almost knocked the tray from my hands. I set it on the table, then patted him and said softly, "Lie down!" Mr. Rochester turned mechanically to see what the commotion was, but since he saw nothing, he returned to his brooding.
"Give me the water, Mary," he said.
I approached him with the now only half-filled glass. Pilot followed me, still excited.
"What is the matter?" he asked.
"Down, Pilot!" I said again. He paused with the glass halfway to his lips, and seemed to listen. He drank, and put the glass down. "This is you, Mary, is it not?"
"Mary is in the kitchen," I answered.

He put out his hand quickly, but not seeing where I stood, he didn't touch me. "Who is this? Who is this?" he demanded, seeming to try to see with those sightless eyes. An expression of pain and bewilderment crossed his face.
"Will you have a little more water, sir? I spilled half of what was in the glass," I said.
"Who is it? What is it? Who speaks?"
"Pilot knows me, and John and Mary know I am here. I came only this evening," I answered.
"Great God!—what delusion has come over me? What sweet madness has seized me?"
"No delusion—no madness. Your mind, sir, is too strong for delusion, your health too sound for madness."
"And where is the speaker? Is it only a voice? Oh! I cannot see, but I must feel, or my heart will stop and my brain will burst. Whatever you are—whoever you are—let me touch you, or I cannot live!"
He groped. I caught his wandering hand and held it in both of mine.
"Her very fingers!" he cried. "Her small, slight fingers! If so, there must be more of her."
The strong hand broke free from mine. My arm was seized, my shoulder—neck—waist—I was pulled close and gathered to him.
"Is it Jane? What is it? This is her shape—this is her size—"
"And this her voice," I added. "She is all here—her heart, too. God bless you, sir! I am glad to be so near you again."
"Jane Eyre!—Jane Eyre," was all he said.
"My dear master," I answered, "I am Jane Eyre. I have found you out—I have come back to you."
"In truth? In the flesh? My living Jane?"
"You touch me, sir. You hold me, and tightly enough. I am not cold like a corpse, nor empty like air, am I?"

"My living darling! These are certainly her limbs, and these her features. But I cannot be so blessed, after all my misery. It is a dream—such dreams I have had at night when I clasped her once more to my heart, just as I do now. And kissed her, as thus—and felt that she loved me, and trusted she would not leave me."
"Which I never will, sir, from this day on."
"Never will, says the vision? But I always woke and found it an empty mockery. And I was desolate and abandoned—my life dark and lonely—my soul thirsting, and the cup always snatched from my lips."
"There, sir—and there!"

I pressed my lips to his once-brilliant, now sightless eyes. I swept the hair from his brow and kissed that too. He suddenly seemed to trust that I was real. A look of grateful joy broke over his worn face.
"It is you—is it, Jane? You have come back to me, then?"
"I have."
"And you do not lie dead in some ditch? And you are not a starving outcast among strangers?"
"No, sir! I am an independent woman now."
"Independent! What do you mean, Jane?"
"My uncle in Madeira is dead, and he left me five thousand pounds."
"Ah! That is practical—that is real!" he cried. "I should never dream that. Besides, there is your particular voice—I could never mistake that. Jane Eyre—Jane Eyre," he repeated.
"Quite rich, sir. If you won't let me live with you, I can build a house of my own close to your door, and you may come and sit in my parlour whenever you want company in the evening."
"But as you're rich, Jane, you must now have friends who will look after you and not let you devote yourself to a blind man like me?"
"I told you I am independent, sir, as well as rich. I am my own mistress."
"And you will stay with me?"

"Certainly—unless you object. I will be your neighbor, your nurse, your housekeeper. I find you lonely. I will be your companion—to read to you, to walk with you, to sit with you, to wait on you, to be eyes and hands to you. Stop looking so gloomy, sir. I will not let you be sad."

He didn't answer right away. He seemed deep in thought—withdrawn. He sighed. He half-opened his lips as if to speak, then closed them again. I felt a kind of panic stir in me. I began to wonder if he was going to refuse me.

"No—no—Jane; you must not go. No—I have touched you, heard you, felt the comfort of your presence—the sweetness of your consolation. I cannot give up these joys. I have little left in myself—I must have you. The world may laugh—may call me absurd, selfish—no matter. My very soul demands you. It will be satisfied, or it will take deadly vengeance on its frame."
"Well, sir, I will stay with you. I have said so."

"Yes—but you understand one thing by staying with me, and I understand another. You perhaps could bring yourself to visit the blind man in his cell and sit beside him—to cheer him—and come again tomorrow. But to consent to stay always with this poor, dark, desolate creature—that is another thing entirely."
"I will think whatever you like, sir. I am content to be only your nurse, if you think it better."
"But you cannot always be my nurse, Janet. You are young—you must marry one day."
"I don't care about being married."
"You should care, Janet. If I were what I once was, I would try to make you care—but—a sightless block!"
He fell back into gloom. I, on the contrary, grew more cheerful and took fresh courage. These last words gave me an opening. I felt it would not do to let the conversation drift into despair.

"It's time someone undertook to bring you back to life," I said, parting his thick, long, uncut hair. "I see you are being turned into a lion, or something of the sort. Your hair reminds me of eagle feathers—whether it has been combed lately I cannot tell."
"On this arm, I have neither hand nor nails," he said, drawing the mutilated limb from his chest and showing it to me. "It is a mere stump—a ghastly sight! Don't you think so, Jane?"
"It is a pity to see it. And a pity to see your eyes—and the scar of fire on your forehead. And the worst of it is, one is in danger of loving you too much for all this and making too much of you."
"I thought you would be revolted, Jane, when you saw my arm and my scarred face."
"Did you? Don't tell me that—or I might say something unflattering about your judgment. Now, let me leave you for a moment to find a better fire than this dead pile of ashes."
"Yes—with the right eye I see a glow—a reddish haze."
"And you see the candles?"
"Very dimly—each is a glowing cloud."
"Can you see me?"
"No, my fairy. But I am grateful enough to hear and feel you."
"When do you have supper?"
"I never have supper."
"But you shall have some tonight. I am hungry—so are you, I expect. Only you've forgotten it."

I called for Mary and soon had the room in better order. I prepared him a comfortable meal. My spirits were high, and I was happy to be active and useful. He seemed astonished, even a little overwhelmed, at the rapid change from loneliness to company, from darkness to warmth.

After supper, he began asking me many questions—where I had been, what I had been doing, how I had found him. But I gave him only brief answers. It was too late for long stories. Besides, I wanted to keep certain things back until another time.
"You are altogether a human being, Jane? You are certain of that?"
"I truly believe so, Mr. Rochester."

"Yet how, on this dark and gloomy evening, could you so suddenly appear at my lonely hearth? I reached out my hand to take a glass of water from a servant, and it was given me by you. I asked a question, expecting Mary's voice to answer—and your voice spoke to my ear."
"Because I had come in, in Mary's place, with the tray."

"And there is enchantment in this very hour I am spending with you. Who can tell what a dark, hopeless life I have dragged through since I last saw you? And suddenly, you appear. I stretch my hand and touch what I dreamed would never be real again."
A plain, practical reply, cutting against the current of his troubled thoughts, was, I was sure, the best comfort I could offer.
"What use is it to do me good, benevolent spirit, when at some moment you will desert me again—passing away like a shadow from my grasp?"
"Have you a pocket comb about you, sir?"
"What for, Jane?"
"Just to comb out this shaggy black mane. I find you rather alarming at close range. You talk of my being a fairy, but I'm sure you look more like a brownie yourself."
"Am I hideous, Jane?"
"Very, sir. You always were, you know."
"Hmph! The mischief hasn't been taken out of you, wherever you've been."
"Yet I have been with good people—far better than you. A hundred times better. People with ideas and views you never entertained in your life. Much more refined, and with much better manners."
"Who on earth have you been with?"
"If you twist around like that, you'll make me pull the hair out of your head. And then I think you'll stop suspecting I'm a phantom."
"Who have you been with, Jane?"
"You won't get it out of me tonight, sir. You must wait until tomorrow. Leaving my tale half-told will, you know, be an excellent way to ensure you let me come back."

"You mocking creature—fairy-born and human-raised! You make me feel as I haven't felt in twelve months. If Saul could have had you for his David, the evil spirit would have been exorcised without the need for a harp."
"There, sir—you're tidied up and made presentable. Now I'll leave you. I have been traveling for three days, and I believe I'm tired. Goodnight."
"Just one word, Jane: were there only ladies in the house where you've been?"
I laughed and made my escape, still laughing as I ran upstairs. "A good idea!" I thought with glee. "I see I have the means of teasing him out of his melancholy for some time to come."

Very early the next morning I heard him up and moving about, wandering from one room to another. As soon as Mary came down, I heard the question: "Is Miss Eyre here?" Then: "Which room did you put her in? Is she up? Go and ask if she wants anything. And when she'll come down."

I came down as soon as I thought breakfast might be ready. I entered the room very softly. I had a view of him before he discovered my presence. He sat in his chair, his old dog at his feet. Pilot's head rested on the mutilated hand—he was trying to caress the animal, but could not manage it well. The look on his face was one of grief and lonely longing—painful, almost unbearable to witness. Yet I held back my tears. This was not a time for tears. I would be upbeat—relentlessly.
"It is a bright, sunny morning, sir," I said. "The rain is over and gone. There is a soft glow after it. You should feel it through the open window. Can you see the light?"
His features lit up at once.

"Oh, you are really there, my skylark! Come to me. You are not gone—not vanished? I heard one of your kind an hour ago, singing high over the wood. But its song had no music for me, any more than the rising sun had brightness. All the melody on earth comes from one voice. All the sunshine from one presence."
The tears stood in my eyes at this confession of his need—just as if a royal eagle, chained to its perch, had been forced to beg a sparrow to be its provider. But I held firm. I would not weep now.

Most of the morning was spent outdoors. I led him out of the wet and wild wood into cheerful open fields. I described the sky and the landscape for him. I let him sit on a comfortable seat and feel the sun. I helped him navigate the uneven ground. I was careful and patient. I was also very happy.

"Cruel, cruel deserter!" he exclaimed at one point. "Oh, Jane, what did I feel when I discovered you had fled from Thornfield? When I couldn't find you anywhere? When, after searching for hours, I knew you were truly gone?"

Prompted by his urgency, I began the story of my experience over the past year. I softened considerably what related to the three days of wandering and starvation—because telling him those things in full would have been torture to him. His loving spirit could not have borne it. The hunger, the cold, the exhaustion—I touched on them lightly, emphasizing instead my rescue.

He said I should not have left him that way, without any means of making my way. I should have told him my intentions. I should have trusted him. He would have found a way to set things right without separation. He swore he would never have forced me to remain at Thornfield. He'd have been happy to know I was safe, even far away.

"Well, whatever my sufferings had been, they were very short," I answered. And then I told him how I had been taken in at Moor House. How I had obtained the position of schoolmistress. The inheritance and the discovery of my relatives followed in due order. Of course, St. John Rivers' name came up frequently. When I had finished, that name was immediately seized upon.
"This St. John, then, is your cousin?"
"Yes."
"You've spoken of him often. Do you like him?"
"He was a very good man, sir. I couldn't help liking him."
"A good man. Does that mean a respectable, well-behaved man of fifty? Or what does it mean?"
"St. John was only twenty-nine, sir."
"Still young, then. Is he a short, dull, plain man? The kind whose goodness lies more in the absence of vice than in any real strength of character?"
"He is tirelessly active. Great and noble deeds are what he lives for."
"But his mind? Probably rather soft? He means well, but you'd shrug listening to him talk?"
"He speaks very little, sir. What he does say is always to the point. His mind is first-rate—not easily swayed, but powerful."
"Is he an able man, then?"
"Truly able."
"A thoroughly educated man?"
"St. John is an accomplished and profound scholar."
"His manners, I think, you said aren't to your taste? Stuffy and preachy?"
"I never mentioned his manners. But unless I have very bad taste, they must suit me. They are polished, calm, and gentlemanly."
"His appearance—I forget how you described it. Some sort of raw young curate, half-strangled by his white collar and tottering on thick-soled boots?"
"St. John dresses well. He is a handsome man—tall, fair, with blue eyes and a Grecian profile."
"Damn him!" (Aside.) Then to me: "Did you like him, Jane?"
"Yes, Mr. Rochester, I liked him. But you asked me that before."

I could see what he was doing, of course. Jealousy had seized him. It stung—but the sting was healthy. It gave him a break from the gnawing fang of melancholy. So I didn't immediately soothe the snake.
"Perhaps you'd rather not sit on my knee any longer, Miss Eyre?" came the next, somewhat unexpected remark.
"Why not, Mr. Rochester?"

"The picture you've just painted suggests a rather overwhelming contrast. Your words have sketched a graceful Apollo—tall, fair, blue-eyed, with a Grecian profile. Your eyes rest on a Vulcan—a real blacksmith, brown, broad-shouldered, and blind and lame into the bargain."
"I never thought of it before, but you certainly do resemble Vulcan, sir."
"Well, you may leave me, ma'am. But before you go"—and he held me with a firmer grip than ever—"just answer me a question or two." He paused.
"What questions, Mr. Rochester?"
Then followed this cross-examination.
"St. John made you schoolmistress of Morton before he knew you were his cousin?"
"Yes."
"You would often see him? He'd visit the school sometimes?"
"Daily."
"He would approve of your plans, Jane? I know they'd be clever, because you are a talented creature!"
"He approved of them—yes."
"He would discover many things in you he hadn't expected? Some of your accomplishments aren't ordinary."
"I don't know about that."
"You had a little cottage near the school, you say. Did he ever come there to see you?"
"Now and then."
"In the evenings?"
"Once or twice."
A pause.
"How long did you live with him and his sisters after the family connection was discovered?"
"Five months."
"Did Rivers spend much time with the women of his family?"
"Yes. The back parlour was both his study and ours. He sat near the window, and we sat by the table."
"Did he study a lot?"
"A good deal."
"What?"
"Hindustani."
"And what did you do in the meantime?"
"I studied German, at first."
"Did he teach you?"
"He didn't know German."
"Did he teach you anything?"
"A little Hindustani."
"Rivers taught you Hindustani?"
"Yes, sir."
"And his sisters too?"
"No."
"Only you?"
"Only me."
"Did you ask to learn?"
"No."
"He wanted to teach you?"
"Yes."
A second pause.
"Why did he want to? What use could Hindustani be to you?"
"He intended me to go with him to India."
"Ah! Now we reach the heart of the matter. He wanted you to marry him."
"He asked me to marry him."
"That's a lie—an outrageous invention to torment me."
"I beg your pardon, it's the plain truth. He asked me more than once, and was just as stubborn about pressing his case as you ever were."
"Miss Eyre, I repeat, you may leave me. How often must I say the same thing? Why do you remain planted on my knee when I've told you to go?"
"Because I'm comfortable here."

"No, Jane, you are not comfortable—because your heart isn't with me. It's with this cousin—this St. John. Oh, until this moment I thought my little Jane was all mine! I believed she loved me even when she left me. That was a drop of sweetness in the bitterness. For all the time we've been apart, for all the hot tears I've wept over our separation, I never imagined that while I was mourning her, she was loving another! But it's only natural enough. You said he was young, handsome, talented. And I—what am I now?"
"Shake me off, then, sir—push me away. I won't leave on my own."
"Jane, I've always loved your voice. It still gives me hope—it sounds so true. When I hear it, it carries me back a year. I forget that you've formed a new attachment. But I'm not a fool—go—"
"Where must I go, sir?"
"Your own way—with the husband you've chosen."
"Who is that?"
"You know—this St. John Rivers."

"He is not my husband, and never will be. He doesn't love me. I don't love him. He loves—as much as he can love, which is not the way you love—a beautiful young woman called Rosamond. He wanted to marry me only because he thought I'd make a suitable missionary's wife, which she would not. He is good and great, but severe. And for me, cold as an iceberg. He is not like you, sir. I am not happy at his side, nor near him, nor with him. He has no hold on my sympathy or warmth. I do not long for his company. I am not drawn to his approval. No warmth rises in me at his approach."
I shuddered involuntarily, and pressed closer to my blind but beloved master. He smiled.
"What, Jane! Is this true? Is this really how things stand between you and Rivers?"

"Absolutely, sir! Oh, you have no reason to be jealous! I wanted to tease you a little, to make you less sad. I thought anger would be better than grief. But if you want me to love you, could you but see how much I do, you would be proud and satisfied. My whole heart is yours, sir. It belongs to you. And with you it would stay, even if fate exiled the rest of me from your presence forever."
Again, as he kissed me, painful thoughts darkened his face.
"My ruined sight! My crippled strength!" he murmured with regret.

I stroked his face to soothe him. I knew what he was thinking and wanted to speak for him, but didn't dare. As he turned away for a moment, I saw a tear slide from under the sealed eyelid and trickle down his cheek. My heart swelled.

"I am no better than the old lightning-struck chestnut tree in Thornfield orchard," he said after a while. "And what right would that ruin have to ask a flowering vine to cover its decay with fresh green?"

"You are no ruin, sir—no lightning-struck tree. You are green and full of life. Plants will grow around your roots whether you ask them to or not, because they delight in your generous shade. And as they grow, they'll lean toward you and wind around you, because your strength offers them the safest support."
Again he smiled. I was giving him comfort.
"You speak of friends, Jane?" he asked.
"Yes, of friends," I answered, somewhat hesitantly. I knew I meant more than friends but couldn't find another word. He helped me.
"Ah! Jane. But I want a wife."
"Do you, sir?"
"Yes. Is that news to you?"
"Of course. You said nothing about it before."
"Is it unwelcome news?"
"That depends on circumstances, sir—on your choice."
"Which you shall make for me, Jane. I'll accept your decision."
"Choose then, sir—her who loves you best."
"I will at least choose—her I love best. Jane, will you marry me?"
"Yes, sir."
"A poor blind man, whom you'll have to lead by the hand?"
"Yes, sir."
"A crippled man, twenty years older than you, whom you'll have to wait on?"
"Yes, sir."
"Truly, Jane?"
"Most truly, sir."
"Oh! My darling! God bless you and reward you!"

"Mr. Rochester, if I ever did a good deed in my life—if I ever thought a good thought—if I ever prayed a sincere and blameless prayer—if I ever wished a righteous wish—I am rewarded now. To be your wife is, for me, to be as happy as I can be on earth."
"Because you delight in sacrifice."

"Sacrifice! What do I sacrifice? Famine for food. Waiting for fulfillment. To be allowed to put my arms around what I treasure—to press my lips to what I love—to rest against what I trust: is that a sacrifice? If so, then yes—I delight in sacrifice."
"And to put up with my weaknesses, Jane. To overlook my flaws."
"Which are nothing to me, sir. I love you better now, when I can truly be useful to you, than I did when you were proud and independent—when you'd accept no role but that of the giver and protector."

"Until now I've hated being helped—being led. From now on, I think I shall hate it no more. I didn't like putting my hand into a hired servant's. But it's a pleasure to feel Jane's little fingers around it. I preferred total loneliness to the constant presence of servants. But Jane's quiet care will be a perpetual joy. Jane suits me. Do I suit her?"
"To the very core of my being, sir."
"Then we have nothing in the world to wait for. We must be married at once."
He looked and spoke with eagerness. His old fire was rising.
"We must be joined without delay, Jane. There's only the license to get—then we marry."
"Mr. Rochester, I've just noticed the sun is well past noon, and Pilot has actually gone home for his dinner. Let me look at your watch."
"Fasten it to your belt, Janet, and keep it. I have no use for it."
"It's nearly four in the afternoon, sir. Aren't you hungry?"
"The third day from now must be our wedding day, Jane. Never mind fine clothes and jewels—none of that matters."
"The sun has dried up all the rain, sir. The breeze is still. It's quite warm."
"Do you know, Jane, I have your little pearl necklace around my neck at this moment, tucked under my collar? I've worn it since the day I lost my only treasure—as a reminder of her."
"We'll go home through the wood. That will be the shadiest way."
He pursued his own thoughts without hearing me.

"Jane! You think me, I'm sure, a godless man. But my heart swells with gratitude to the merciful God of this earth right now. He sees not as man sees, but far more clearly. He judges not as man judges, but far more wisely. I did wrong. I would have stained my innocent flower—breathed guilt on its purity. The Almighty snatched it from me. I, in my stubborn rebellion, nearly cursed the punishment. Instead of bowing to the decree, I defied it. Divine justice followed its course. Disasters came thick upon me. I was forced to pass through the valley of death. His punishments were heavy. I acknowledged their justice. I began to experience remorse, repentance, the wish for reconciliation with my Maker. I began sometimes to pray—brief prayers, but very sincere."

"Some days ago—four days, to be exact—last Monday night, a strange mood came over me. Grief replaced frenzy. Sorrow replaced bitterness. I had long been convinced that since I couldn't find you anywhere, you must be dead. Late that night—perhaps between eleven and midnight—before going to my miserable bed, I begged God, if it pleased Him, to take me soon from this life and admit me to the next world, where there was still hope of reunion with Jane."

"I was in my room, sitting by the open window. The mild night air soothed me. I could see no stars—only by a faint, luminous haze did I know the moon was out. I longed for you, Janet! Oh, I longed for you with soul and flesh! I asked God, in anguish and humility, whether I had not been desolate and tormented long enough. Whether I might not soon taste peace and happiness again. I admitted I deserved everything I'd endured. I could hardly expect mercy. But I begged for it—urgently. Then I cried out: 'Jane! Jane! Jane!'"
"Did you speak those words aloud?"
"I did, Jane. If anyone had heard me, they'd have thought me insane. I said them with such desperate force."
"And it was last Monday night, near midnight?"

"Yes. But the time doesn't matter. What followed is the strange part. You'll think me superstitious—there's some superstition in my blood, and always has been. But this is true—at least it is true that I heard what I'm about to tell you.

"As I cried 'Jane! Jane! Jane!' a voice—I cannot tell where it came from, but I know whose voice it was—replied, 'I am coming: wait for me.' And a moment later, the wind carried a whisper: 'Where are you?'

"Let me try to describe what those words created in my mind—though it's hard to express. Ferndean is buried, as you see, in heavy woodland where sound falls flat and dies without echo. 'Where are you?' seemed spoken among mountains. I heard a hill-sent echo repeat the words. At that moment the wind felt cooler and fresher on my brow. I could have believed that, in some wild, lonely place, Jane and I were meeting. In spirit, I believe we must have met. You—wherever you were—must have felt it at the same moment."

Reader, it was on Monday night—near midnight—that I too had received the mysterious call. Those were the very words with which I had answered it. I listened to Mr. Rochester's account but said nothing in return. The coincidence struck me as too strange and awe-inspiring to discuss. If I told anything, my story would inevitably make a deep impression on his mind—and that mind, already too prone to dark thoughts from suffering, did not need the added weight of supernatural mystery. I kept these things in my heart.

"You can't wonder, then," my master continued, "that when you appeared before me so unexpectedly last night, I had difficulty believing you were anything more than a voice and a vision—something that would dissolve into silence, as the midnight whisper and mountain echo had dissolved before. Now, I thank God! I know otherwise. Yes, I thank God!"

He set me down from his knee, rose, and reverently lifted his hat from his head. Bending his sightless eyes toward the earth, he stood in silent devotion. Only the last words of his prayer were audible.
"I thank my Maker that, in the midst of judgment, He has remembered mercy. I humbly beg my Redeemer to give me strength to lead a purer life than I have lived until now!"

Then he reached out his hand to be led. I took that dear hand, held it a moment to my lips, then let it rest around my shoulder. Being so much shorter than he, I served as both his support and his guide. We entered the wood and made our way home.
